‘Ah, Papa, you have never managed to arrange that, and I don’t believe you ever will. Isabella cannot stand being left behind when her husband goes.’

This was too plainly true to dispute. Unwelcome though it was, Mr. Woodhouse could only sigh in resignation. Seeing how the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband lowered his spirits, Emma immediately turned to an aspect of the subject that would restore them.

‘Harriet must spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I’m sure she will enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, aren’t we, Papa? I wonder which she will think better-looking, Henry or John.’

‘Yes, I wonder which. Poor little dears, they will be so glad to come. They are very fond of Hartfield, Harriet.’

‘I’m sure they are, sir. I certainly can’t think of anyone who isn’t.’

‘Henry is a fine boy, but John looks very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest, named after me rather than his father. John, the second, has his father’s name. I believe some people are surprised that the eldest wasn’t named after him, but Isabella insisted on Henry, which I thought very sweet of her. And he is a very clever boy indeed. They are all remarkably clever, and do so many charming things. They come and stand beside my chair and say, “Grandpapa, can you give me a piece of string?” Once Henry asked for a knife, but I told him knives were made only for grandpapas. I often think their father is too rough with them.’

‘He seems rough to you,’ Emma said, ‘because you are so gentle yourself. If you compared him with other fathers, you wouldn’t think so. He wants his boys to be active and strong, and when they misbehave he can speak sharply now and then. But he is a loving father—Mr. John Knightley is certainly a loving father. All the children are fond of him.’

‘And then their uncle comes in and throws them up toward the ceiling in that dreadful way!’

‘But they enjoy it, Papa; they like nothing better. It gives them such pleasure that if their uncle didn’t insist they take turns, whichever one went first would never make room for the other.’

‘Well, I cannot understand it.’

‘That is true of all of us, Papa. Half the world cannot understand what gives the other half pleasure.’

‘Oh, naturally your father can spare you if your mother can. Daughters never matter quite so much to a father. And if you remain another full month, I shall be able to convey one of you as far as London, since I go there early in June for a week. Dawson has no objection to the barouche-box, so there will be ample space for one—and indeed, should the weather be cool, I would not object to taking both of you, for neither is very large.’

‘You are most kind, madam; but I think we must keep to our first arrangement.’

Lady Catherine appeared to acquiesce. ‘Mrs. Collins, you must provide a servant to accompany them. You know I always say what I think, and I cannot endure the thought of two young women travelling post alone. It is exceedingly improper. You must find someone to send. I dislike that kind of thing above everything. Young ladies ought always to have suitable protection and attendance, according to their station. When my niece Georgiana visited Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two men-servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not properly have appeared in any other fashion. I pay the closest attention to such matters. You must let John travel with these young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am pleased I remembered to raise it, for allowing them to go alone would truly reflect ill upon you.’

‘My uncle is sending a servant to meet us.’

‘Oh, your uncle! So he employs a man-servant? I am delighted that someone considers these matters. Where do you intend to change horses? At Bromley, naturally. Mention my name at the Bell and you will receive attention.’

Lady Catherine had numerous further inquiries concerning their journey, and since she did not supply every answer herself, they required attention. Elizabeth thought this fortunate; otherwise, with her mind so preoccupied, she might have forgotten her surroundings. Reflection had to wait for hours of solitude. Whenever she was alone, she surrendered to it with the greatest relief, and each day included a solitary walk in which she could enjoy all the pleasure of painful recollections.

She was well on the way to learning Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. Every sentence received her study, and her feelings towards its author varied greatly. Recalling the manner of his proposal, she remained indignant; but considering the injustice with which she had judged and reproached him, she directed her anger at herself instead, and felt compassion for his disappointed hopes.

What, then, follows from this? What idea have I brought before your imagination?’

My flesh crept as Dupin put the question. ‘A madman,’ I answered, ‘committed this act—some raging lunatic who escaped from a neighbouring asylum.’

‘In certain respects,’ he responded, ‘your notion is not beside the point. But even in their most violent fits, the voices of madmen never resemble that singular voice heard on the staircase. Madmen belong to some nation, and however disordered their words, their speech retains an orderly division into syllables. Moreover, a madman’s hair does not resemble what I am holding. I drew this small tuft from Madame L’Espanaye’s tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it.’

‘Dupin!’ I exclaimed, utterly shaken. ‘This hair is extraordinary—it is not human hair.’

‘I have never maintained that it was,’ he replied; ‘but before settling that question, I would have you examine this little sketch I have made on the paper. It reproduces exactly what one part of the evidence calls “dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails” on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and another, supplied by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne, describes as a succession of livid marks plainly impressed by fingers.

‘You will notice,’ my friend continued, laying the sheet before us on the table, ‘that the drawing suggests a steady and unyielding grip. No slipping is visible. Every finger maintained—perhaps until the victim died—the terrible hold in which it first sank into the flesh. Now try placing all your fingers simultaneously upon the corresponding marks shown here.’

I tried, without success.

‘Perhaps we have not conducted a fair experiment,’ he observed. ‘This sheet lies upon a flat surface, whereas a human throat forms a cylinder. Here is a piece of wood approximately equal to the throat in circumference. Wind the drawing round it and make another attempt.’

I obeyed, but found the difficulty still more apparent. ‘This,’ I declared, ‘cannot be the impression of a human hand.’

‘Now read this passage in Cuvier,’ Dupin answered.

It contained a detailed anatomical and general description of the great tawny orangutan of the East Indian Islands. The enormous size, astonishing strength and agility, savage ferocity, and tendency to imitation of these mammals are familiar enough to everyone. I comprehended immediately the whole horror of the murder.

‘The account of the fingers,’ I said, finishing the passage, ‘agrees precisely with your drawing.
